Confucius identified seventy-seven disciples proficient in the six arts, categorizing them by virtue (Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, Zhong Gong), political skill (Ran You, Ji Lu), eloquence (Zaiwo, Zigong), and erudition (Ziyou, Zixia). He noted individual traits: Zhuan Sun was extreme, Zeng Shen slow, Gao Chai stupid, Zhong You rude, and Yan Hui poor. Zigong, rejecting fate, became a successful merchant. Confucius respected figures like Laozi, Zang Boyu, Yan Zhongping, Laolaizi, Zichan, and Meng Gongchuo, and praised others from earlier eras. ================================================================================
Yan Hui (Yan Yuan), thirty years younger than Confucius, was praised for virtue, living frugally without changing his joy. Confucius said he restrained himself to conform to etiquette, was not stupid, and shared a philosophy of serving when employed and hiding when not. Yan Hui died prematurely at twenty-nine, causing Confucius great grief. Duke Ai of Lu was told Yan Hui was the best learner, never transferring anger or repeating mistakes. ================================================================================
Min Ziqian, fifteen years younger, was deemed exceptionally filial, avoiding official service. Ran Boniu suffered an incurable disease; Confucius lamented his fate. Zhong Gong, asked about governance, was advised to be courteous and cautious; Confucius deemed him fit for high office despite his humble father. Ran Qiu, twenty-nine years younger, managed military affairs for the Ji family; Confucius encouraged his timidity. Zilu (Zhong You), nine years younger, was bold and straightforward, initially bullying Confucius but later becoming a disciple. Confucius taught him to prioritize righteousness over bravery, and he died in Wei during a rebellion, tying his hat before death. ================================================================================
Zaiwo, eloquent, questioned the three-year mourning period, suggesting one year sufficed; Confucius rebuked him for lacking benevolence. Zaiwo later died in a rebellion in Qi. Zigong, thirty-one years younger, was articulate and wealthy. Confucius compared him to a vessel and praised his humility. Zigong’s diplomatic mission saved Lu, disrupted Qi, destroyed Wu, strengthened Jin, and enabled Yue’s dominance, altering the balance of power among states. ================================================================================
Ziyou, forty-five years younger, governed Wucheng with music and ritual; Confucius joked about using a “knife to kill a chicken” but later praised him. Zixia, forty-four years younger, discussed the Book of Songs with Confucius, who noted his slight deficiency. After Confucius’s death, Zixia taught in Hexi. Zizhang, forty-eight years younger, learned about gaining office through caution and about achieving success through loyalty and respect. Zeng Shen, forty-six years younger, understood filial piety and wrote the Book of Filial Piety. ================================================================================
Other disciples included Tantai Mieming, initially judged poorly by appearance but later renowned; Mi Zijian, praised as a gentleman; Yuan Xian, who valued poverty over shame; Gongye Chang, married to Confucius’s daughter; Nangong Kuo, praised for morality; and Gao Chai, deemed stupid. Youruo, resembling Confucius, was briefly treated as a teacher but failed to answer questions. The text lists thirty-five disciples with recorded ages and deeds, and forty-two without, concluding that later accounts vary, with the author relying on The Analects for accuracy. ================================================================================

The king of Nanyue, Wei Tuo (Zhao Tuo), was from Zhending. During the Qin dynasty, after conquering the six states, the Qin annexed Yang Yue, establishing Guilin, Nanhai, and Xiangjun, and resettled criminals there to live with the Yue people for thirteen years. Zhao Tuo served as the magistrate of Longchuan County in Nanhai. In the second year of the Qin dynasty, Ren Xiao, the captain of Nanhai, fell ill. He summoned Zhao Tuo and explained that with Chen Sheng’s rebellion and the Qin’s cruel policies, the Central Plains were in chaos. He noted that Nanhai was remote and could be defended by mountains and sea, and suggested Zhao Tuo could establish a state. Ren Xiao appointed Zhao Tuo as acting captain. After Ren Xiao’s death, Zhao Tuo cut off roads, gathered troops, killed Qin-appointed officials, and replaced them with his cronies. Following the Qin’s fall, he annexed Guilin and Xiangjun and declared himself King Wu of Nanyue. ================================================================================
Emperor Gaozu of Han, due to the people’s exhaustion, spared Zhao Tuo. In the eleventh year of Gaozu, he sent Lu Jia to confirm Zhao Tuo as King of Nanyue, with an agreement for envoys and harmony with Baiyue. During Empress Lü’s reign, officials banned ironware trade with Nanyue. Zhao Tuo suspected King Changsha’s influence, declared himself Emperor Wu of Nanyue, and attacked Changsha’s border cities. Empress Lü sent General Zhou Zao to attack, but heat and illness halted the army. After her death, the Han stopped. Zhao Tuo expanded his territory to over 10,000 miles, bribing Minyue, Xiou, and Luoyue, and acted as an emperor. ================================================================================
In the first year of Emperor Wen of Han, the emperor honored Zhao Tuo’s parents’ tomb and his cousins. He sent Lu Jia to rebuke Zhao Tuo for claiming the emperor title. Zhao Tuo apologized, citing fear of King Changsha and the queen’s actions, and claimed he used the title for self-comfort among barbarians. He pledged vassalage to Han, removed imperial trappings, and continued as a vassal. During Emperor Jing’s era, Zhao Tuo outwardly submitted but secretly kept the emperor title. He died in the fourth year of Jianyuan, succeeded by his grandson Zhao Hu. ================================================================================
Zhao Hu faced an attack from Minyue’s King Ying. He requested Han intervention, and Emperor Wu sent troops, leading to Ying’s death. Zhao Hu thanked the emperor but, advised by ministers, avoided visiting the capital, fearing captivity. He died as King Wen. His son Yingqi, who had married a woman from Handan and fathered Zhao Xing, became king. Yingqi hid his grandfather’s emperor seal, refused to visit the capital due to fear of Han laws, and died as King Ming. Zhao Xing succeeded, with his mother as queen mother. ================================================================================
The queen mother, who had previously committed adultery with Anguo Shaoji, sought to submit to Han. Emperor Wu sent Anguo Shaoji to persuade them. The young king and queen mother agreed to become vassals, but Prime Minister Lu Jia, who had served three kings and held great influence, opposed. He feared losing power and plotted rebellion. At a banquet, the queen mother tried to provoke the Han envoy to kill Lu Jia, but the envoy hesitated. Lu Jia left, gathered troops, and refused to meet the king. The queen mother’s efforts failed. ================================================================================
The emperor sent Han Qianqiu with 2,000 troops to South Vietnam. Lu Jia rebelled, killed the king, queen mother, and Han envoys, and installed Zhao Jiande as king. Han Qianqiu’s army was ambushed and destroyed. The emperor then launched a large-scale attack in the fifth year of Yuanding, with generals Lu Bode, Yang Pu, and others leading forces from multiple directions. In the sixth year, Yang Pu’s troops captured Panyu, and Lu Bode’s forces accepted surrenders. Lu Jia and Zhao Jiande fled by sea but were captured. South Vietnam was pacified, and the Han established nine counties. The kingdom lasted five generations for ninety-three years. The historian notes that Zhao Tuo’s rise was due to Ren Xiao, and the kingdom’s fall stemmed from internal conflicts and Lu Jia’s actions. ================================================================================

Wei Qing, a native of Pingyang County, was the illegitimate son of Zheng Ji and a concubine of the Pingyang Marquis household. His half-sister Wei Zifu gained favor with Emperor Wu of Han, leading Wei Qing to adopt the surname Wei. As a youth, he served as a servant and shepherd, enduring mistreatment from his half-brothers. A prisoner once prophesied his future nobility, but Wei Qing dismissed it. He later became a cavalryman for the Pingyang Marquis. ================================================================================
When Wei Zifu entered the palace and became pregnant, Empress Chen, jealous, attempted to kill Wei Qing. His friend Gongsun Ao rescued him, and Emperor Wu subsequently appointed Wei Qing as a palace supervisor, elevating his status. Wei Zifu later became empress, and Wei Qing was promoted to Dazhong doctor. ================================================================================
In 129 BCE, Wei Qing led a cavalry attack on the Xiongnu, achieving modest success. Subsequent campaigns saw him capture the Henan region, driving out Xiongnu kings and establishing Shuofang Commandery. For these victories, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Changping. Further campaigns against the Xiongnu resulted in significant victories, including the capture of King Youxian's forces and vast numbers of livestock. Emperor Wu granted Wei Qing additional households and enfeoffed his sons as marquises, though Wei Qing humbly declined, crediting the emperor and his officers. ================================================================================
Wei Qing's nephew, Huo Qubing, emerged as a brilliant commander, earning the title of Champion Marquis for his daring raids. Huo Qubing's campaigns were marked by deep penetrations into Xiongnu territory, capturing kings and vast numbers of enemies. He became increasingly favored by the emperor, eventually matching Wei Qing in rank and power. Huo Qubing famously declined a mansion, stating, "The Xiongnu have not yet been eliminated, so I have no intention of considering private matters." However, he was known for his lack of concern for his soldiers' welfare, often discarding food while they starved. ================================================================================
After Huo Qubing's death, Wei Qing's influence waned. Wei Qing died four years later, and his descendants lost their titles due to legal infractions. The text concludes with a list of Wei Qing's and Huo Qubing's subordinates, many of whom became generals or marquises. The historian Sima Qian notes that Wei Qing, despite his nobility, refrained from recruiting scholars, fearing the emperor's displeasure, a principle Huo Qubing also followed. ================================================================================

Sima Ranju, a descendant of Tian Wan, was recommended by Yan Ying to Qi Jinggong during a crisis when Jin and Yan attacked Qi. Despite his humble status, Ranju’s literary and military talents impressed the king, who appointed him general. Ranju requested a trusted minister, Zhuang Jia, to supervise the army. They agreed to meet at the camp gate at noon. Ranju arrived early and set up timing devices, but Zhuang Jia, delayed by farewell feasts, arrived at dusk. Ranju condemned his lateness, citing that a general must forsake family, friendships, and personal safety in war. He executed Zhuang Jia under military law, shocking the army. ================================================================================
When Qi Jinggong’s envoy arrived with a pardon, racing into camp, Ranju declared that generals in the field need not accept all royal orders. He executed the envoy’s servants and horses, parading them before the troops. Ranju then personally cared for soldiers, sharing provisions and tending to the sick. After three days, the army was revitalized. The Jin and Yan forces withdrew upon learning of this discipline, and Qi reclaimed lost territory. ================================================================================
Returning in triumph, Ranju was appointed Grand Sima by Qi Jinggong, elevating the Tian family’s status. However, officials Bao, Gao, and Guo slandered him, leading to his dismissal and death from illness. The Tian family later retaliated, killing the Gao and Guo clans. Tian He, a descendant, became King Qi Wei, who imitated Ranju’s methods and incorporated his strategies into the “Sima’s Art of War.” Sima Qian notes that while Ranju’s achievements were for a small state, the “Sima’s Art of War” is profound, and he refrains from further commentary, presenting only this biography. ================================================================================

Lu Buwei, a wealthy merchant from Yangzhai, amassed a fortune through low-cost buying and high-price selling. During the reign of King Zhao of Qin, the crown prince died, and An Guojun was appointed as the new prince. An Guojun had many sons, including Zichu, a middle-ranking son sent as a hostage to Zhao. Zichu, neglected and impoverished, caught Lu Buwei's attention. Lu Buwei traveled to Qin to lobby An Guojun and his favored concubine, Mrs. Huayang, who had no son. He persuaded Mrs. Huayang to adopt Zichu as her heir, ensuring her future influence. The historian Tai Shigong reflects on Mencius, noting that King Hui of Liang’s focus on profit troubled him, as Confucius rarely discussed profit to prevent resentment. Mencius, a student of Zisi’s disciples, failed to gain favor with King Xuan of Qi or King Hui of Liang, who found his ideals impractical. During an era of reforms—where states like Qin, Chu, Wei, and Qi thrived through figures like Shang Yang, Wu Qi, and Sun Bin—Mencius advocated ancient virtues, which did not align with the prevailing strategies of alliances and warfare. He returned home to compile the *Mencius* with Wan Zhang. ================================================================================
After Mencius, Zou Yan emerged in Qi, observing princes’ decadence and developing theories on yin-yang and the five virtues (metal, wood, water, fire, earth). His writings, such as *The End and the Beginning*, were vast and speculative, tracing history from the present to before heaven and earth formed. He divided the world into nine continents like Chixian Shenzhou, surrounded by seas, and linked dynastic changes to cosmic cycles. Despite their grandiosity, his ideas emphasized benevolence and frugality, impressing rulers like King Zhao of Yan, who treated him with high respect—unlike Confucius and Mencius, who faced hardship. ================================================================================
Other scholars included Chunyu Kun of Qi, known for his wit and ability to read minds; he remained silent before King Hui of Liang until the king focused on governance, later conversing for three days but declining a prime minister post. Shen Dao, Tian Pian, and Jiezi wrote on Huang-Lao doctrines, while Zou Shi expanded on Zou Yan’s work. The King of Qi honored these scholars with high positions and grand residences to attract talent. ================================================================================
Xunqing of Zhao, at age fifty, lectured in Qi, criticizing Zou Yan’s empty theories and Chunyu Kun’s cleverness. He became the eldest Jixia scholar, serving as Lanling magistrate in Chu after slander in Qi. His student Li Si became Qin’s prime minister. Xunqing condemned chaotic times and was buried in Lanling. Other figures like Gongsun Long, Hui Shi, Li Kui, and Mo Zhai—who advocated defense and cost-saving—also contributed to the era’s diverse philosophies. ================================================================================

A comprehensive historical overview of the evolution of criminal law and punishment in ancient China, emphasizing the tension between benevolent governance and strict legal enforcement. It begins by contrasting ideal governance through etiquette, which fosters integrity, with reliance on criminal law, suggesting that the era of Emperor Wu was inferior to the Fuxi clan's time. The narrative underscores that natural principles govern human emotions and actions, and that benevolent policies, like those of Yao and Shun, should precede punishment to maintain harmony. ================================================================================
The text traces the development of legal systems from the Zhou Dynasty, which respected heaven's mandate and used a mix of rewards and punishments, through the Qin Dynasty's harsh laws, which led to widespread suffering. The Han Dynasty, under Liu Bang and Emperor Wen, initially adopted lenient measures, but later emperors like Emperor Wu and Emperor Xuan saw fluctuations in legal severity. The text notes that during the Han, legal codes expanded significantly, with over 26,000 rules and 7.7 million words, leading to confusion and inconsistency. ================================================================================
Key figures like Liang Tong and Chen Chong advocated for legal reform, arguing against excessive leniency and for balanced punishments. Liang Tong criticized the proliferation of laws that reduced the death penalty, leading to a disregard for crime, while Chen Chong proposed aligning punishments with the ancient "Fu Xing" code, which specified 3,000 types of punishments. Despite these efforts, reforms were often stalled by political turmoil and differing opinions among officials. ================================================================================
The text also discusses the debate over corporal punishment, with proponents like Liu Song arguing that it would deter crime more effectively than imprisonment or death, while opponents like Kong Rong contended that it would not prevent evil and would permanently stigmatize offenders. The Wei and Jin dynasties saw further legal codification, with the Wei Code creating 18 chapters and the Jin Code expanding to 21 chapters, aiming to simplify and standardize laws. ================================================================================
Throughout, the text highlights the challenges of maintaining a consistent and fair legal system, with frequent changes in laws and interpretations leading to confusion and injustice. It concludes by noting that despite ongoing debates and attempts at reform, such as those during the Jin Dynasty's move south, the implementation of corporal punishment and other legal changes remained contentious and often unrealized. ================================================================================

Wang Mao, courtesy name Xiuyuan, was born in Qi, Taiyuan. His grandfather Wang Shen served as Beizhonglang Sima, and his father served as a general in the late Song Dynasty, defeating Situ Yuancan at Shitou and becoming prefect of Brazil and Zitong counties. As a child, Wang Mao was valued by his grandfather, who predicted he would establish the family. He grew to eight feet tall with a white and beautiful face, calm and reserved by nature, and fond of military books. ================================================================================
During the late Song and Ming Dynasties, Wang Mao served in various military positions. When Wei general Li Wunu invaded, Wang Mao marched westward. After the Wei army retreated, he served as Sima of Zhennan and later as Yue Cavalry School captain. When Wei invaded Yanzhou, he served as General Shi of Ningshuo. In the early Jianwu years, he rescued Sizhou from Wei siege and followed Gaozu to defeat Wei generals. After the Wei retreat, he became chief minister of the auxiliary state and governor of Xiangyang. ================================================================================
When Emperor Gaozu raised a righteous army, Wang Mao consulted with Zhang Hongce about welcoming Emperor He, but Gaozu disagreed. Wang Mao served as vanguard, pacifying Jiahu and defeating Guangzijin and Wu Ziyang, beheading tens of thousands. After Jiankang City was pacified, he became general guarding the army, then Shizhong and leading general. He was granted the title of Duke of Wangcai County with 2,300 households. In the first year of the Han Dynasty, he conquered the rebellious Chen Bozhi. He later served as right servant of Shangshu, general of chariots and cavalry, and Kaifu Yitong Sansi. He died at sixty, receiving posthumous honors and the title Zhonglie. ================================================================================
Cao Jingzong, courtesy name Zizhen, was a new savage. His father Cao Xinzhi was a military general in the Song Dynasty. Young Cao Jingzong excelled at horseback archery and hunting. At twenty, while traveling alone with few followers, he was surrounded by hundreds of barbarians but fought them off with arrows, gaining fame for courage. He loved reading history books, particularly admiring Rang Ju and Le Yi. ================================================================================
During the Southern Qi Dynasty, Cao Jingzong served as prefect of Tianshui and fought against barbarian uprisings. He showed loyalty by retrieving the body of his friend Zhang Daomen after Zhang's father was killed. In the Jianwu years, he fought against Northern Wei invasions, defeating Tuoba Ying's 40,000 reinforcements with 2,000 ambush soldiers. He became close friends with Xiao Yan (Emperor Wu of Liang) when Xiao served as governor of Yongzhou. ================================================================================
When Emperor Wu raised troops, Cao Jingzong gathered his forces and served as vanguard, besieging Yingcheng for months until surrender. He advanced toward Jiankang, defeating Li Jushi at Jiangning despite his troops' worn equipment. After the city fell, he was made Marquis of Xiangxi County with 1,600 households. In the Tianjian years, he was promoted to General Pingxi and Marquis of Jingling County. During the Northern Wei invasion of Sizhou, he was impeached for not sending timely rescue but was protected by Emperor Wu. ================================================================================
In the fifth year, when Tuoba Ying invaded Zhongli, Cao Jingzong led rescue forces. Despite imperial orders to wait, he attempted to advance alone but was turned back by storms. He eventually joined Wei Rui at Shaoyangzhou, building fortresses near Wei positions. In the sixth year, during spring floods, they launched a coordinated attack, burning Wei camps and causing massive casualties. Over 50,000 Wei soldiers were captured alive, with countless supplies seized. Cao Jingzong was promoted to Duke with 2,000 households. ================================================================================
Cao Jingzong was self-reliant and proud, showing respect only to Wei Rui. He was a womanizer with hundreds of concubines, impatient and restless, fond of drinking and hunting. He died at fifty-two while traveling to assume the governorship of Jiangzhou. ================================================================================
Liu Qingyuan, named Wenhe, was born in Hedong Jie. He served as chief administrator of Yingzhou and prefect of Wei Xing, where he handled a flood wisely. Emperor Gaozu recruited him as a historian, and Qingyuan became a loyal strategist during Gaozu's rebellion. After Jiankang was pacified, he served as minister and was deeply trusted by Gaozu, who entrusted him with palace keys during a fire. ================================================================================
After Gaozu ascended the throne, Qingyuan became Marquis of Chong'an with 1,000 households. He served as governor of Yongzhou, where Emperor Gaozu praised him for eliminating western concerns. He later returned to Kyoto and served in various high positions. He died at fifty-seven while serving as governor of Yongzhou again, receiving posthumous honors and the title Zhonghui. ================================================================================

Zang Dun began his career as Fu Junxing to join the army, later becoming Shangshu Binglang. He was known for his handsome appearance and elegant manners, which pleased Emperor Gaozu. He served as Zhongshu General Secretary Shiren and An Youlushi. His filial piety was evident when he felt a sudden pain in his finger the night his mother died, leading him to mourn for five years in a thatched hut, becoming emaciated. He was appointed Sanqi Changshi and later leader of the army, handling military affairs with intelligence and courage. He died in 543 at age 66, posthumously honored as Attendant. ================================================================================

Yao Cha praised Fu Qi's foresight, noting that if his advice had been heeded, the Taiqing chaos might have been avoided. ================================================================================

Since the Han Dynasty's founding, sycophants and favored ministers who gained imperial favor through flattery appeared regularly. During Emperor Gaozu's reign, there was Ji Ru; under Emperor Xiaohui, there was Hong Ru. Neither possessed outstanding talents, relying solely on flattery to gain wealth and favor. They accompanied the emperor closely, influencing even ministers who used them to communicate with the throne. Their impact was so great that Emperor Hui's officials adopted their customs, decorating hats with delicate feathers, belts with seashells, and applying makeup—a trend attributed to figures like Ji Ru and Hong Ru. Both became wealthy and noble in their lifetimes, later moving to Anling. ================================================================================
Subsequent favored figures included Deng Tong, eunuch Zhao Tan, and Beigong Bozi under Emperor Wen; Han Yan and eunuch Li Yannian under Emperor Wu; eunuchs Hong Gong and Shi Xian under Emperor Yuan; Zhang Fang and Chun Yuchang under Emperor Cheng; and Dong Xian under Emperor Ai. Emperors Jing, Zhao, and Xuan had no notable favorites, though Zhou Ren under Emperor Jing, Jin Shang under Emperor Zhao, and Peng Zu under Emperor Xuan received some favor without causing harm. ================================================================================
Deng Tong, from Nan'an in Shu, was known as Huangtoulang for wearing a yellow hat while rowing. Emperor Wen once dreamed of ascending to heaven but was unable until a yellow-headed man pushed him upward. After waking, the emperor sought the man and found Deng Tong, whose clothing matched the dream. Delighted, the emperor favored him greatly, rewarding him with tens of thousands in cash and high office. Deng Tong was cautious and solemn, avoiding outsiders even during holidays. A fortune-teller predicted he would die poor and hungry, but the emperor, confident in his power, gave him Tongshan Mountain in Shu to mint coins, making Deng Tong immensely wealthy. When Emperor Wen developed abscesses, Deng Tong sucked them with his mouth. The emperor asked who loved him most, and Deng Tong replied the prince. The prince, uncomfortable with sucking the sores, later resented Deng Tong. After Emperor Wen's death, Emperor Jing dismissed Deng Tong. Accused of minting coins outside, Deng Tong was convicted, his property confiscated, and he died penniless in another's home. ================================================================================
Zhao Tan gained favor through astrology, and Beigong Bozi through elder-like generosity, but neither matched Deng Tong. Han Yan, grandson of Gonggaohou Qidang, studied with Emperor Wu during his youth. After Emperor Wu became emperor, Han Yan's skills in horseback riding and archery, along with his intelligence, earned him favor comparable to Deng Tong. He often slept and rose with the emperor. Once, while hunting, King Jiangdu mistook Han Yan's entourage for the emperor and knelt, but Han Yan passed without noticing. The king complained to the empress dowager, who hated Han Yan thereafter. When adultery rumors reached her, she had Han Yan killed despite the emperor's pleas. Han Yan's brother, Han Shuo, also favored, was later killed during the witchcraft disaster. ================================================================================

Empress Xu bribed Chun Yuchang to regain favor, but he deceived her. Wang Mang, fearing Chun Yuchang's rise, exposed his crimes to Wang Gen and the empress dowager. Their property was confiscated, and his family exiled. The text concludes that these favored ministers, lacking virtue, met bad ends, and their rise contributed to the Western Han's decline. ================================================================================

Du Zhou, a native of Du Yan County in Nanyang, rose from being an assistant to Governor Yi Zong to an official historian under Zhang Tang. He gained the emperor's trust by convicting and executing many during investigations of border counties, serving as Zhongcheng for over a decade. Taciturn and slow-tempered but kind-hearted, Du Zhou succeeded Xuan as Tingwei, modeling his governance after Zhang Tang and adeptly reading the emperor's intentions. He would frame those the emperor wished to exclude and prolong imprisonment for those the emperor wished to forgive, secretly revealing their grievances. When criticized for not following established laws, Du Zhou argued that laws were created by monarchs and should adapt to current circumstances. As Tingwei, he handled over a thousand cases annually, with large cases involving hundreds of witnesses. Many fled or hid upon hearing of impending arrests, and cases could drag on for over a decade through multiple amnesties. Prisons held 60,000 to 70,000 criminals, with ordinary officials adding up to 100,000. Du Zhou was later deposed but returned as Jinwu, harshly pursuing thieves and interrogating Sang Hongyang's sons and Queen Wei's brothers. Promoted to imperial censor, his family wealth accumulated to hundreds of millions. His two sons served as governors, but only his youngest, Du Yannian, was kind-hearted. ================================================================================

Suihong, courtesy name Meng, was from the state of Lu. Initially fond of cockfighting and horse racing, he later transformed his character and studied the "Spring and Autumn" with Ying Gong. Through his mastery of Confucian classics, he became a Yilang and reached the position of Fuli Jieliang. ================================================================================
In the first month of the third year of Emperor Zhao's Yuanfeng reign, a great roar was heard south of Laiwu Mountain in Mount Tai. A large stone stood up by itself, measuring one to five feet high, as thick as forty-eight arm spans, and eight feet deep into the ground, with three other stones serving as its feet. Thousands of white crows gathered around it. Simultaneously, dead trees in the Changyi Shrine revived, and a broken willow in Shanglin Garden stood up and regained life, with insects eating its leaves into shapes resembling the words "Gongsun Bing has been established." Suihong interpreted these events through the "Spring and Autumn," concluding that stones and willows symbolized common people, while Mount Tai represented the site of imperial ceremonies. He argued that these phenomena indicated commoners would become emperors and the deposed Gongsun clan would revive. He advocated for the Han emperor to abdicate in favor of a worthy successor. His friend, an internal official, submitted this memorial. Since Emperor Zhao was young and General Huo Guang governed, Huo Guang was angered and had Suihong and his friend executed for treason. Five years later, when Emperor Xiaoxuan rose from the people to the throne, he recruited Suihong's son as a Lang. ================================================================================

His nephew Xiahou Sheng, courtesy name Changgong, was also a renowned Confucian scholar. Xiahou Sheng lost his father young but studied diligently, learning "Shang Shu" and "Hong Fan's Five Elements" from Shichang, and later studied under Jian Qing and Ouyang. He was sophisticated and learned from multiple teachers. ================================================================================
When King Changyi succeeded Emperor Zhao, he frequently traveled. The king was furious and had him bound, but Huo Guang did not punish him. When Huo Guang and Zhang Anshi were discussing deposing the king, Xiahou Sheng explained his prediction came from the "Hong Fan" biography, which stated that when an emperor rules improperly, subordinates will rebel. Huo Guang and Anshi were impressed and valued Confucian scholars more thereafter. They eventually petitioned the Queen Mother to depose King Changyi and establish Emperor Xuan. Xiahou Sheng was appointed Shaofu of Changxin and given the title of Marquis of Guannei. ================================================================================
When Emperor Xuan wanted to honor Emperor Wu's achievements, Xiahou Sheng opposed, arguing that although Emperor Wu defeated barbarians and expanded territory, he killed many ministers, exhausted resources, and caused widespread suffering and cannibalism. The ministers impeached Xiahou Sheng for slandering the late emperor, and he was imprisoned. After an earthquake killed over six thousand people, Emperor Xuan issued a general amnesty, and Xiahou Sheng was pardoned and served as an admonition official. He was known for his forthrightness, addressing the emperor as "king" and calling colleagues by name in court. Emperor Xuan trusted him for this honesty. Xiahou Sheng died in office at ninety, and the Queen Mother mourned him for five days. ================================================================================
Jingfang, courtesy name Junming, studied "The Book of Changes" under Jiao Yanshou. Jiao Gan, his teacher, was known for predicting evil events and governing Xiaohuang County well. During Emperor Yuan's reign, he predicted events accurately and was frequently consulted. He warned about disasters and criticized the appointment of flattering officials like Shi Xian. Jingfang recommended implementing a system to inspect officials' performance, but faced opposition from powerful ministers. He was eventually appointed prefect of Wei County but feared being isolated from the emperor. After sending several sealed memorials warning about yin energy overwhelming yang and predicting disasters, he was imprisoned and executed at age forty-one. ================================================================================
Yi Feng, courtesy name Shaojun, studied "Qi Shi" and was diligent in learning, preferring calendar and yin-yang divination to officialdom. Emperor Yuan respected him greatly. Yi Feng wrote extensively about using the twelve laws to understand human emotions and predict disasters. He warned about the dangers of powerful relatives and advocated for frugality, criticizing excessive palace construction. He proposed moving the capital to Chengzhou to reform institutions and reduce expenses. Although Emperor Yuan found his views unusual, Yi Feng became a doctor and admonishing official, dying in old age. ================================================================================
Li Xun, courtesy name Zichang, studied "Shangshu" and liked theories of disasters and strange phenomena. He served under various officials and warned about impending floods and chaos. During Emperor Ai's reign, he was summoned to discuss disasters and advised restraining relatives, selecting virtuous officials, and following seasonal orders. He later supported Gan Zhongke's forged texts about the Han dynasty's fate declining, advocating for changing the reign name to prolong the dynasty. Huo Guang, courtesy name Zimeng, was the younger half-brother of the renowned general Huo Qubing. Their father Zhongru served as a county official in the Pingyang Hou family and had an affair with the maid Wei Shaoer, fathering Huo Qubing. After completing his duties, Zhongru returned home, married, and fathered Huo Guang, severing all ties with Wei Shaoer. When Huo Qubing later learned of his father's identity while serving as a hussar general attacking the Xiongnu, he visited Zhongru in Hedong, purchased lands and slaves for him, and took ten-year-old Huo Guang to Chang'an. Huo Guang was appointed as Lang and later promoted to various positions. After Huo Qubing's death, Huo Guang served as Guanglu and Commander-in-Chief, accompanying Emperor Wu for over twenty years with cautious conduct, earning the emperor's complete trust. ================================================================================
As Emperor Wu aged and Prince Wei was defeated, the emperor chose his young son as heir and entrusted Huo Guang with assisting him. He gave Huo Guang a painting of Duke Zhou carrying King Cheng, symbolizing his expectations. When Emperor Wu fell ill at Wuzha Palace, he appointed Huo Guang as Grand Sima General, along with Jin Rixi, Shangguan Jie, and Sang Hongyang as co-regents. After Emperor Wu's death, the eight-year-old Emperor Zhao ascended the throne, with Huo Guang making all political decisions. Huo Guang was calm, thoughtful, and meticulous in his conduct, maintaining consistent positions when entering and leaving the palace gates. ================================================================================
Huo Guang's daughter married Shangguan Jie's son Shangguan An, whose daughter became Emperor Zhao's empress. However, conflicts arose when Huo Guang refused to grant titles to Ding Wairen, a favorite of the Grand Princess Eyi Gaizhu. Shangguan Jie, his son, Sang Hongyang, and the Grand Princess conspired with King Liu Dan of Yan, sending a false letter accusing Huo Guang of arrogance and improper conduct. Emperor Zhao, only fourteen, saw through the deception, noting that the letter mentioned events that occurred only ten days prior, which King Yan could not have known. The conspirators then plotted to assassinate Huo Guang, but their scheme was discovered. Huo Guang executed Shangguan Jie, Shangguan An, Sang Hongyang, Ding Wairen, and their families, while King Yan and the Grand Princess committed suicide. ================================================================================
After Emperor Zhao died without an heir, the ministers initially considered King Liu Xu of Guangling, but Huo Guang opposed this due to the king's immoral character. Following a suggestion from a Lang official citing historical precedents, Huo Guang arranged for the installation of King Liu He of Changyi. However, Liu He soon began behaving lewdly and improperly. Huo Guang, troubled by this, consulted with Tian Yannian, who cited the precedent of Yi Yin deposing Taijia. Huo Guang gathered the ministers, and after Tian Yannian threatened those who hesitated with execution, they agreed to depose the king. Huo Guang reported to the Empress Dowager, who issued an edict. The ministers jointly impeached King Changyi for numerous offenses during his twenty-seven-day reign, including failing to observe mourning, engaging in debauchery, and issuing over 1,127 orders for various items. The Empress Dowager approved the deposition, and Huo Guang personally removed the imperial seal from King Changyi, who was sent back to his former residence. ================================================================================
Huo Guang then arranged for the installation of Emperor Wu's great-grandson, who was living among the people, as Emperor Xuan. For his services, Huo Guang received additional fiefdoms totaling 20,000 households, along with gold, money, silk, slaves, and horses. His family members held numerous important positions throughout the court. Huo Guang remained in power for twenty years until his death, after which he was buried with great honors at Maoling and given the title Xuanchenghou. ================================================================================
After Huo Guang's death, his wife Xian and their sons Huo Yu, Huo Yun, and Huo Shan became increasingly arrogant and extravagant. Xian had previously poisoned Empress Xu to install her daughter as empress, a secret that Huo Guang had concealed. As Emperor Xuan gradually reduced the Huo family's power, they grew fearful and plotted rebellion, planning to depose the emperor and install Huo Yu. The conspiracy was discovered, leading to Huo Yun, Huo Shan, and Fan Mingyou committing suicide, while Xian, Huo Yu, and others were executed. The Huo clan was exterminated, and Empress Huo was deposed. ================================================================================
Jin Rixi, originally a Xiongnu prince, was captured as a slave after his father King Xiutu was killed. He served as a horse keeper but caught Emperor Wu's attention through his dignified bearing and honest answers. He became a trusted attendant, known for his loyalty and filial piety. He killed his own son for improper behavior with palace servants and later helped thwart a rebellion by Mang Heluo. When Emperor Wu appointed regents, Jin Rixi served as Huo Guang's deputy, refusing a marquisate due to Emperor Zhao's youth. His descendants continued serving the Han court for seven generations, maintaining a reputation for loyalty and filial piety. ================================================================================

A comprehensive system of astronomical and calendrical calculations, beginning with a series of defined numerical constants and methods. The "method number" is derived from multiplying the original Huang Zhong Chujiu by itself. The "leap method" of nineteen is used as the number of years in a chapter. The "Tongfa" (1,539) is obtained by multiplying the leap number by the daily number, and the "Yuanfa" (4,617) is three times the Tongfa. Other key numbers include the "Zhang month" (235), "Moon Dharma" (2,392), and "Weekly days" (562,120). The text details the calculation of various astronomical cycles, including the synodic meeting, meeting months, and the cycles of the year star, Taibai Star, Zhenxing, Yinghuo, and the stars (Mercury). For each planet, the text provides specific numbers for its appearance, motion (direct, retrograde, and stationary), and the duration of its visibility and concealment, along with the degrees it travels. ================================================================================
The text then outlines methods for deducing the Sun-Moon Yuan Tong, calculating the winter solstice, and determining the positions of the five stars. It describes how to calculate the number of years since the original Shangyuan and the specific cycles of Jiazi, Jiachen, and Jiashen. Procedures are given for calculating the first day of the lunar month, the location of the leap remainder, and the twenty-four solar terms. The text also details the calculation of the stars' positions at morning and midnight, the lunar eclipse, and the complex numbers for the manifestation of the five stars. It explains how to determine the middle number of a star's appearance, the star and the moon, and the degree of the next day after entering the center. ================================================================================
The text provides a detailed breakdown of the five steps of calculation for the planets, using the number of days since their first appearance and their daily motion. It also describes the calculation of the age (Sui Xing) and its profits and losses, noting that the Sui star's misplacement can cause disasters. The text then lists the twelve celestial divisions (Xingji) from Dou Twelve Degrees to Dou Shidu, associating each with a solar term and the corresponding months in the Xia, Shang, and Zhou calendars. It provides the degrees for various constellations and explains the cycles of nine ends and three ends, which relate to the unification of the calendar. ================================================================================
The text includes a historical chronology, starting from the legendary emperors (Taiwu, Yandi, Huangdi, Shaowu, Zhuan Xu, Xue, Tang, Yu) and their associated virtues (wood, fire, earth, metal, water). It traces the lineage and reigns of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties, providing specific years and astronomical events. For example, it notes that the Xia dynasty had 432 years, the Shang dynasty 629 years, and the Zhou dynasty 867 years. The text also details the reigns of the Qin dynasty and the early Han emperors, from Gaozu to Emperor Guangwu, providing the number of years for each reign and the total years since the Shangyuan. It concludes with the reign of Emperor Guangwu, noting that he reigned for 33 years. ================================================================================

The "Book of Xia" records Yu's thirteen-year flood control efforts, during which he passed his home without entering. He traveled by various means—car, boat, sled, or sedan—to delineate Kyushu's boundaries, dredge rivers, and assess land for taxation. Despite his work, the Yellow River continued to devastate the Central Plains. Yu prioritized managing it, guiding its waters from Jishi Mountain through Longmen and other locations, but its turbulent flow proved difficult to tame. He eventually split the river into two to reduce its force. After Kyushu's rivers and lakes were stabilized, the benefits extended to the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties. The Yellow River was later diverted southeast, intersecting with several rivers and countries. ================================================================================
In various regions, canals were built for irrigation and transport. In Chu, ditches connected Moshui and Yunmeng; in Wu, canals linked three rivers and five lakes; in Qi, the Zi and Jishui rivers were joined. In Shu, Li Bing dug two rivers in Chengdu to prevent flooding. These canals facilitated boat travel and irrigation, bringing prosperity. During Wei Wenhou's reign, Ximen Bao governed Ye County with a good reputation, but his successor Shi Qi criticized him for not using the Zhangshui River for irrigation. Shi Qi then diverted the Zhangshui to irrigate Ye County, making the area fertile. Later, the Qin state employed Zheng Guo, a Han spy, to build a canal from the Jingshui River. Though initially suspected, Zheng Guo convinced Qin of the canal's long-term benefits. During the Han dynasty, the Yellow River burst multiple times. In Emperor Xiaowen's reign, it broke at Suizao, and later during Yuanguang, it breached at Huzi, flowing into Juyeze and the Huai River. Attempts to block it failed, and Tian Ju advised against further efforts, citing divine will. Zheng Dangshi proposed a canal from Chang'an to divert the Wei River, reducing transport time and irrigating farmland. Despite initial inaction, a major breach in Guantao flooded 32 counties. Wang Yanshi successfully blocked it, earning rewards. Later breaches required further efforts, with Yang Yan and others involved. Debates over river management continued, with some advocating for relocating people and opening canals, while others favored minimal intervention. During Wang Mang's reign, various experts proposed strategies, but none were implemented. The text concludes by emphasizing the Yellow River's significance and the need for careful study of water management. ================================================================================

The principles of the "Six Classics" share a common goal, with the functions of "Li" (ritual) and "Yue" (music) being particularly urgent. For individuals, forgetting propriety leads to evil and contempt; for a state, losing it brings desolation and disorder. Ritual and music are made according to the laws of heaven and earth to communicate with gods, establish human ethics, and regulate all things. Specific rituals, such as those for marriage, drinking in the countryside, mourning, and meeting the emperor, are formulated to address human nature and prevent specific vices. Confucius stated that there is no better way to stabilize a country and govern the people than propriety, and no better way to change customs than music. When etiquette, music, government orders, and criminal laws all function smoothly, the kingly way is complete. The two are used together to create harmony and respect. ================================================================================
The Zhou Dynasty learned from the Xia and Yin Dynasties, creating a particularly complete etiquette system with 300 major rituals and 3,000 details. This led to widespread education, harmony, and a lack of disasters for over forty years. When the Zhou Dynasty declined, princes exceeded the law and deleted relevant documents. The Qin Dynasty then destroyed various schools, causing rituals and music to be scattered. After the Han Dynasty was established, Emperor Gaozu ordered Shusun Tong to formulate etiquette. Emperor Wen was pleased with Jia Yi's proposals to establish rituals, but ministers Zhou Bo and Guan Ying were jealous, so his suggestions were not adopted. Emperor Wu's plans were dropped due to Empress Dowager Dou's preference for Taoism. Dong Zhongshu argued that heaven advocates virtue over punishment, and that the Han Dynasty must change its education to reform the people. Emperor Xuan did not adopt Wang Ji's suggestion to select Confucian scholars and inherit old etiquette. Liu Xiang persuaded Emperor Cheng to build Piyong and arrange rituals and music, but the emperor died before the plan was completed. Wang Mang later built Piyong to confuse people and usurp the throne. ================================================================================
Emperor Guangwu established Mingtang and Biyong after thirty years of rule. However, moral education was not widespread because rituals and music were not in place. The rituals written by Shusun Tong were recorded with laws and collected by judges, but not passed down by Legalists. Music is loved by saints for its power to change people's minds. The former kings formulated the music of Yasong based on human emotions and the principles of music, coordinating with yin and yang to guide the five constants. Before composing music, emperors would use the music of their ancestors to teach the people. Various ancient emperors created specific pieces of music, such as Huangdi's "Xianchi" and Shun's "Shao." The "Shao" music was preserved in the state of Chen. Confucius, after hearing "Shao" in Qi, did not know the taste of meat for three months. During the Zhou Dynasty's decline, the music of Sangjian, Pushang, Zheng, and Wei appeared, causing internal disease and external political harm. After the Han Dynasty's establishment, Shusun Tong used musicians from the Qin Dynasty to produce music for the ancestral temple.
